**The useful lesson is a bias–sample-efficiency tradeoff, not a universal logarithmic sample rule.** Naive Bayes imposes a strong structure on how features relate within a class. That structure can make its estimates stabilize quickly with limited data, but it can also constrain the best boundary it will ever reach. [1](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2001/hash/7b7a53e239400a13bd6be6c91c4f6c4e-Abstract.html)

Logistic regression directly fits the conditional decision problem. It may require more examples to estimate its boundary well while eventually achieving a lower limiting error when the generative assumptions are wrong.

**Think of two learning curves.** One descends quickly and levels off at a higher error; another descends more slowly and eventually passes it. This illustrates the result's intuition without claiming that every dataset follows those curves. If Naive Bayes assumptions are well matched or the discriminative model is misspecified, the comparison can differ.

The Ng–Jordan analysis concerns particular model pairs and assumptions, with feature dimension and sample count playing different roles. Reusing n for both obscures the claim. Read the stated theorem before quoting asymptotic rates, and validate the practical choice with learning curves under consistent features, regularization, and held-out evaluation.

**Technical details and references.**

The Ng–Jordan result compares particular generative/discriminative pairs under specific assumptions and uses dimension/sample complexity carefully; the prompt's single symbol $n$ conflates feature dimension with sample count. It is not a universal $O(\log n)$ guarantee for arbitrary Naive Bayes data. [1](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2001/hash/7b7a53e239400a13bd6be6c91c4f6c4e-Abstract.html)

The practical insight is that strong generative assumptions can reach their own limiting error quickly, while a discriminative model may approach a better asymptotic boundary more slowly. If Naive Bayes assumptions are wrong, its bias persists; if they are correct, the comparison changes. Evaluate learning curves at several sample sizes and report assumptions rather than applying the slogan as a theorem about every dataset.
